notes.meaning: Ezra fell to the ground outside the temple, weeping and confessing the nation's sins to God. His open grief touched the people deeply, causing a large crowd of men, women, and children to gather around him and weep aloud. Their shared tears showed that the people were beginning to feel the weight of their own disobedience.

Shecaniah spoke up on behalf of the gathered people, admitting that they had broken faith with God by marrying pagan women from neighboring lands. Even though his own father and uncles were guilty of this sin, he boldly proclaimed that Israel still had hope. That hope rested on God's willingness to show mercy if they turned away from their sin.

Shecaniah proposed making a covenant, which is a solemn and binding promise before God, to send away the foreign wives and their children. Because these pagan marriages violated God's law and pulled families into idol worship, breaking them off was seen as the only way to restore the nation's spiritual purity. He urged that everything be handled in careful obedience to the law of Moses.

differ.view: Reformed teachers note that while this separation was necessary to preserve Israel, Christians today are commanded not to divorce an unbelieving spouse who is willing to remain married.
Many evangelicals teach that this crisis belonged to a specific time in Israel's calling as an isolated holy nation, and Christians cannot use this passage to justify divorce.

notes.meaning: Shecaniah told Ezra to stand up and take charge, reminding him that God had given him the duty to lead this reform. He promised that the leaders and the people would stand behind him and give him full support. He encouraged Ezra to be courageous and take immediate action.

Ezra got up from the ground and made the high priests, Levites, and community leaders take a sacred oath to carry out Shecaniah's proposal. The leaders all swore the oath, binding themselves before God to follow through. This step made sure the rulers could not back out once the difficult work began.

Ezra left the public courtyard in front of the temple and went into a private side room belonging to Jehohanan. While there, he practiced a complete fast, refusing to eat bread or drink water because of his deep sorrow over the people's unfaithfulness. True leadership often carries the spiritual pain of others before God in secret prayer.

The leaders sent an official order throughout the towns of Judah and Jerusalem, calling all the returned exiles to gather at the capital. The territory of the returnees was small enough that everyone could hear the message and make the journey. The whole community needed to be present to deal with this national failure.

The proclamation warned that anyone who did not arrive within three days would lose all their property, which would be handed over to the temple. In addition, the offender would be cast out of the assembly, losing their rights and status as an Israelite. The leaders set these strict rules to make sure no one ignored the call to repent.

All the men of Judah and Benjamin gathered in Jerusalem within the three days and sat in the open square in front of the temple. It was late December, the coldest and rainiest time of the year in Palestine. The entire crowd sat shivering from both the freezing downpour and the terrifying knowledge of their guilt before God.

Ezra stood up in the middle of the shivering assembly and addressed them plainly. He charged them with being unfaithful to God by marrying pagan foreign women, which added fresh guilt to a nation that had already suffered so much in exile. Idolatry in family life threatened to destroy the spiritual survival of the entire community.

Ezra commanded the crowd to confess their sins to the Lord, the God of their ancestors, and to obey His will. Real repentance meant that they had to separate themselves from the surrounding pagan peoples and send away their foreign wives. A genuine confession before God always requires turning away from the wrong behavior.

The entire gathering shouted their agreement in a single, loud voice. They admitted that Ezra was right and promised that they must do everything he commanded. Their unified answer showed that they understood the danger of God's anger and were willing to submit to His law.

The people pointed out that standing outdoors in the freezing winter rain was impossible for such a massive crowd. Furthermore, so many families had broken the law that sorting out every single case would take far more than a day or two. They asked for a practical and orderly way to carry out the investigation.

The assembly suggested setting up an official council in Jerusalem made up of their top leaders. Men who had married foreign wives could travel from their hometowns at assigned times, accompanied by their local elders and judges who knew the local facts. This careful process would continue until every case was resolved and God's anger was turned away.

Only four men, led by Jonathan and Jahzeiah with two Levites supporting them, opposed the community's plan. Scripture does not say why they objected, but their small number shows how strongly the rest of the nation supported the reform. The overwhelming majority was ready to follow Ezra and obey God's commands.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Older English versions translated this verse to say these four men were appointed to manage the process, but modern scholars read the Hebrew as stating that they stood in opposition to the plan.

notes.meaning: The returned exiles carried out the plan just as they had promised. Ezra selected respected family leaders by name to sit as judges, setting aside all other tasks to focus solely on this matter. They convened their court on the first day of the tenth month to begin examining every family case.

The judges spent three full months investigating every situation with great care. By the first day of the first month, which was the start of the new Jewish year, they had finished examining every man who had married a foreign woman. Their thorough work brought a clean and orderly end to the community's national failure.

The record begins the list of offenders with the priests, revealing that even the religious leaders had failed to keep God's law. Four descendants from the family of Jeshua, the first high priest to return from Babylon, were found to have married foreign wives. When leaders compromise with sin, it easily spreads to the rest of the community.

These guilty priests shook hands in a solemn pledge, promising to divorce and send away their foreign wives. They also offered a ram as a guilt offering, an animal sacrifice prescribed by the law to make amends and seek God's forgiveness. By confessing and sacrificing first, the priests set a necessary example of repentance for the entire nation.

These verses name thirteen more priests who had married foreign women, belonging to the ancestral families of Immer, Harim, and Pashhur. Together with Jeshua's family, these were the four major priestly clans that had originally returned from Babylon. Listing their names publicly showed that no family, no matter how influential or holy their office, was excused from accountability before God.
